newsitem.title: INDIA: First half profits of Indian firms badly hit - study.
newsitem.headline: First half profits of Indian firms badly hit - study.

text.p: First half results of Indian companies announced so far have shown a modest 4.0 percent growth in net profit and a 2.1 percent fall in earnings, a study found on Thursday.
"Profitability has taken a beating," said R. Balakrishnan, president at securities firm Dil Vikas Finance Ltd in his analysis.
The study includes a sample of 181 firms which announced results until November 19. Market capitalisation of these companies totals around $30 billion.
Sectors which emerged outperformers in the analysis were hotels, auto, auto ancilliaries, refining and housing finance.
Balakrishnan said second half performance would be largely dependent on commodity prices in the remaining part of 1996/97 (April-March).
"Interest rates have also not declined across-the-board as the prime lending rate (PLR) reduction benefits just a handful of companies," he said.
Most Indian banks cut their PLR by 0.5-1.5 percentage points after India's central bank eased liquidity in its monetary policy last month.
Balakrishnan said weak capital markets were likely to impact those companies which were in the midst of setting up new capacities.
"With all this in mind, we could actually see a negative EPS growth for the full year," he said.
Sales of companies in the six months to September 30, 1996 rose by an aggregate 18 percent, the study found.
"However this has been skewed by the weak sales growth in the PSUs (state-run firms), seven of which account for nearly 23 percent of the sales," Balakrishnan said.
"The smaller companies and multinationals have recorded the highest growth in sales, with the GDR companies' sales growing at a fairly impressive 20 percent," he said.
The analysis classified companies by their ownership patterns (state-run, multinationals, GDR and others), except for the finance sector which formed a separate group.
Balakrishnan said EBDIT (earnings before depreciation, interest and tax) but excluding other income grew 19 percent, showing that operating margins had not dropped significantly.

He said net profit had been hit by slower growth in "other income," implying use of surplus funds in assets and working capital. A 32 percent jump in depreciation charges over the year ago indicated an increase in asset base.

"This is a positive factor for the future as it indicates capitalisation of newer production facilities. In fact, of the last four years, this increase is the highest in terms of real depreciation charge," Balakrishnan said.
A whopping 46 percent jump in interest costs reflected higher borrowings as well as higher interest rates.
Balakrishnan said profits of multinational companies had increased by 15 percent. GDR companies had fared the worst.
"The GDR companies have been the worst performers with their absolute profits actually declining by 1.0 percent," Balakrishnan said.
-- Priya Ramani, Bombay newsroom +91-22-265 9000
